newsitem.title: USA: Democrats to block subpoenas on funds.
newsitem.headline: Democrats to block subpoenas on funds.

text.p: The top Democrat on a Senate committee investigating campaign fund-raising scandals has said he will block the issuance of all new subpoenas by the Republican majority, political sources said Monday.
Ohio Sen. John Glenn made the threat in a letter to Tennessee Republican Sen. Fred Thompson, chairman of the Senate governmental affairs committee.

Glenn followed up by blocking the issuance of a subpoena requested by Thompson last week and demanding a committee meeting where he can air his concerns. A meeting was likely later this week, where the disagreement will become public.

The committee was investigating whether China and other foreign interests sought to influence U.S. foreign policy by helping President Bill Clinton and the Democratic Party with illegal political contributions.
The Democratic Party has promised to return some $3 million which were apparently illegally raised from foreign interests, mainly Asian corporations and businessmen.

Democrats would like to probe Republican financial links to foreign business interests. The Republicans have returned some $122,000 raised for a party think tank from a Hong Kong company and Democrats believe they have much more to hide.

Thompson can overcome Glenn's objections by holding party-line votes in the committee where the Republicans have a 9-7 majority. But he is anxious to preserve a bipartisan tone to the investigation if he can.

However, Thompson was beginning to believe that the White House has decided to try to discredit his committee as it prepares to for public hearings, which will probably begin early next month, the sources said.

In his letter, Glenn protested at what he called the "gross imbalance" in the issuance of subpoenas by the committee, which he said had mainly targeted Democrats and their allies and ignored Republicans.

In a second letter, Glenn also objected to the dispatch of a team of investigators to Asia to interview witnesses. Glenn said the trip was a waste of taxpayers' money because only two witnesses had agreed to meet the investigators. Republican sources said Glenn was wrong on that point.
Sources close to the committee said some key Democratic officials had refused to answer important questions from investigators. If they persist, Thompson will consider taking legal steps.

When hearings do begin, Thompson was considering summoning some key witnesses even though they have said they would invoke their Fifth Amendment rights not to testify. They would then have to refuse to answer questions in public view.
Many key players in the scandal have either gone to Asia or indicated their intention of "taking the Fifth."

The latest to do so were 16 Buddhist monks who received subpoenas from the committee last month. Their temple hosted a fund-raising event last year addressed by Vice President Al Gore, in possible violation of its tax exempt status as a religious institution.
